## The senior bar

What separates a senior answer from a mid-level one in this area.

- Picks the least autonomous design that solves the task (single call, workflow, agent) and justifies it with error compounding, cost per task and cost of a wrong action.
- Treats the model as an untrusted proposer, so permissions, argument validation, budgets, idempotency and approvals are enforced in code outside the model and never only in the prompt.
- Reasons about context as a budgeted, cache-sensitive compiled state and can say what goes in, in what order, what is compacted and what is fetched on demand.
- Separates retrieval failures from generation failures in RAG, measures each stage, and knows hybrid retrieval, reranking and permission filtering concretely.
- Changes prompts, tools and models as versioned changes gated by a regression eval, and debugs incidents from traces rather than from guesses.
- Quantifies cost and latency per completed task (input and output tokens, cache hit rate, time to first token, steps per task) and knows which lever moves which number.
- Can scope work with a customer down to one measurable workflow, define acceptance criteria and carry it from demo to production.

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-001">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What is an agent, concretely? Walk me through the loop and tell me which parts belong to the model and which to your code.</summary>

An agent is a model run in a loop where the model, not the code, picks the next action from
what it has observed so far. It has four parts:

- **Model**: proposes either a final answer or one or more tool calls.
- **Tools**: typed functions the harness can execute (search, read, write, run code).
- **State**: the message history plus anything kept outside the window (plan, files, event log).
- **Stop condition**: the model answers without a tool call and the completion check passes,
  or a budget (steps, tokens, wall-clock, money) runs out, or the run needs a human, or a
  fatal error occurs.

One iteration: compile context from state, call the model, and if it requested tools then
validate the arguments, check permissions, execute, append the bounded result as an
observation and repeat.

The split that matters: the model owns judgment under ambiguity (which hypothesis to test,
what is missing, how to read an unfamiliar error). Code owns invariants (step limits, schema
validation, timeouts, permission checks, approval for destructive actions). A model proposal
is not a side effect until the harness has parsed, authorised and executed it. If the control
flow is fixed in code and the model only fills in steps, it is a workflow, not an agent.

**Follow-ups**

- Which stop conditions would you enforce in code even if the prompt already states them?
- What does the model see when a tool call fails?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-002">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> When does a fixed workflow beat an agent, and when is an agent worth it?</summary>

Use the least autonomy that solves the task. A single call for classification, extraction or
Q&A; a workflow (code-defined steps, model fills each one) when the steps are known in
advance; an agent only when the path depends on what is discovered along the way.

Why not default to an agent:

- **Compounding error.** If each step succeeds independently with probability $p$, an
  $n$-step run succeeds with about $p^n$: $0.95^{20} \approx 0.36$, $0.99^{20} \approx 0.82$.
  This is a pessimistic bound only when the environment gives feedback the agent can use to
  recover (tests, error messages); silent errors compound fully.
- **Cost and latency.** Every step re-sends the growing history, so uncached input tokens
  grow roughly quadratically in the number of steps.
- **Predictability.** A workflow has enumerable paths that can be tested and audited.

An agent earns its cost when four things hold: the task is open-ended and hard to specify
as steps; the outcome is valuable enough to pay for many calls; the model is actually good
at the task; and errors are cheap to detect and undo (tests, review, rollback).

The common production shape is a hybrid: code fixes the outer stages and the invariants,
and the model makes local decisions or runs a bounded loop inside one stage.

**Follow-ups**

- Give an example you would build as a workflow that a team wanted to build as an agent.
- How does a verifier change the $p^n$ argument?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-003">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Single agent or multiple agents? When do sub-agents help and what do they cost?</summary>

Start with one agent. Add sub-agents for a specific reason, not to mirror an org chart.

What sub-agents buy:

- **Context isolation.** A sub-agent can read 100k tokens of search results or files in its
  own window and return a 1-2k token finding, keeping the lead's context clean.
- **Parallelism.** Independent sub-tasks run concurrently and cut wall-clock time.
- **Specialisation.** Different tool sets, prompts or cheaper models per role.
- **Independent checking.** A reviewer that has not seen the author's reasoning is less
  anchored on it.

What they cost:

- **Tokens.** Each sub-agent pays for its own context; total usage is typically several
  times a single agent's.
- **Lossy hand-offs.** The sub-agent knows only the brief, and the lead sees only the
  summary. Errors come back in the same confident tone as findings.
- **Coordination.** Parallel agents that make interdependent decisions produce conflicts
  (two agents editing the same file, incompatible assumptions).

Good fit: breadth-first, read-heavy, separable work (research across sources, codebase
search, per-document extraction). Poor fit: tightly coupled writing where every decision
depends on shared context.

Rules that make it work: give each sub-agent an explicit brief (goal, what is already ruled
out, output format, tool and scope limits); have it return compact, checkable results or
pointers to artefacts; keep writes single-threaded; cap depth and fan-out.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you measure whether a multi-agent version is worth its token cost?
- What goes wrong if the lead forwards its own hypothesis in the brief?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-004">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Name the common orchestration patterns for LLM systems and say when each fits and how it fails.</summary>

| Pattern | Shape | Fits when | Typical failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prompt chain | fixed sequence, each call consumes the previous output, with code checks between | task decomposes into known steps | an early error propagates; latency adds up |
| Router | classify the input, dispatch to a specialised prompt, tool set or model | distinct request types with different handling | misroutes fail silently; needs per-route evals |
| Parallel fan-out | split into independent parts, or run the same task several times and vote | separable sub-tasks, or a need for higher confidence | merge step loses or duplicates content; cost multiplies |
| Orchestrator-workers (planner-executor) | a lead model decomposes at run time and delegates to workers | sub-tasks are not known in advance | bad decomposition; plan not revised when evidence changes |
| Evaluator-optimizer | a generator proposes, an evaluator critiques against criteria, loop until pass or budget | clear criteria and measurable gain from revision | evaluator is too lenient or the loop never converges |
| Autonomous loop | model chooses tools until done | open-ended tasks with good environment feedback | wandering, loops, runaway cost |

Two points interviewers look for. First, these compose: a router in front of a chain, with
one stage being a bounded agent loop. Second, plans should be mutable: plan, act briefly,
observe, replan beats executing a long fixed plan, because later steps depend on
observations the planner did not have. An evaluator should check the artefact or the
environment (tests, schema, citations), not just ask the same model whether it is happy.

**Follow-ups**

- Where would you put deterministic checks in a prompt chain?
- When does voting across samples actually improve accuracy?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-005">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Your agent sometimes runs until it hits the step limit without finishing. How do you investigate and what do you change?</summary>

Read the traces of the runs that ended on the budget and classify them before changing
anything. The usual causes:

1. **Repeated identical call.** The tool returns an error the model cannot act on
   ("failed"), or the result never reaches the model (tool result not paired with its call
   id, or truncated to nothing), so it retries the same thing.
2. **Oscillation.** Two fixes that undo each other, common when a verifier reports failure
   without saying what failed.
3. **No reachable stop.** The definition of done is missing or the completion check can
   never pass (flaky test, impossible requirement).
4. **Lost state.** Compaction dropped the fact that an approach was tried and failed.
5. **Unbounded exploration.** Pagination or search with no convergence criterion.

Changes, in order:

- Make errors actionable: what failed, why, and what input would be valid.
- Detect loops in code: hash (tool, normalised arguments); after k repeats inject a notice,
  force a replan, or stop.
- Hard budgets on steps, tokens and wall-clock, with a graceful exit that reports partial
  progress instead of an exception.
- Give the model an explicit way out: "cannot complete, here is why" or ask the user.
- Keep failed attempts and unresolved errors verbatim through compaction.

Then monitor the termination-reason histogram and the steps-per-task distribution (p50,
p95), and add the looping cases to the regression set.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you tell a legitimate long task from a loop?
- The loop detector fires on a polling tool. What do you do?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-006">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Design a customer-support agent for an e-commerce company that can answer questions and perform actions such as refunds.</summary>

**Clarify first.** Channels (chat, email, voice), volume, top intents, which actions are in
scope, policy sources, the target (resolution rate at equal or better CSAT) and the cost of
a wrong action.

**Architecture.**

1. *Intake*: authenticate the customer, attach account context, run input checks.
2. *Routing*: a small model classifies intent and risk; out-of-scope or sensitive intents go
   straight to a human.
3. *Knowledge*: RAG over help-centre and policy documents, with document versions and
   effective dates, so policy answers are grounded and cited.
4. *Agent loop with tools*: read tools (order status, shipment, account) run freely; write
   tools (refund, cancel, address change) are gated.
5. *Escalation*: hand off with a structured summary (issue, steps taken, customer data
   gathered) so the human does not start over.

**Controls outside the model.** Tools take the authenticated customer id from the session,
never from model arguments, and the backend re-checks ownership. Refunds carry an
idempotency key; amounts above a limit, or repeated refunds, require human approval. Policy
limits live in code. Customer messages and ticket text are untrusted input. PII is redacted
in logs.

**Evaluation.** Offline: a golden set of conversations per intent, simulated multi-turn
users, graders for policy adherence, correct tool use and groundedness. Online: resolution
rate, reopen rate within 7 days, CSAT, escalation rate and its precision, cost per resolved
conversation.

**Rollout.** Shadow mode, then draft-for-human, then autonomous on low-risk intents, then
expand intent by intent.

**Failure modes to name.** Inventing policy, premature "resolved" to hit the metric,
social-engineering for refunds, loops with frustrated users (cap turns and escalate).

**Follow-ups**

- How do you stop the agent from promising something the policy does not allow?
- Which metric would the team game first, and what counter-metric do you add?
- What changes for the voice channel?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-007">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Write a minimal agent loop with tool calling against a generic chat-completions-style client. Then tell me what is missing for production.</summary>

Assume `client.chat(messages, tools)` returns
`{"content": str | None, "tool_calls": [{"id", "name", "arguments": <JSON string>}], "finish_reason": str}`.

```python
import json
import jsonschema

def run_agent(client, system, user_msg, tools, max_steps=20):
    """tools: {name: {"description": str, "parameters": <JSON Schema>, "fn": callable}}"""
    specs = [{"name": n, "description": t["description"], "parameters": t["parameters"]}
             for n, t in sorted(tools.items())]            # stable order keeps the prefix cacheable
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system},
                {"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        reply = client.chat(messages=messages, tools=specs)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply["content"],
                         "tool_calls": reply["tool_calls"]})
        if reply["finish_reason"] == "length":
            raise RuntimeError("output truncated; tool arguments may be incomplete")
        if not reply["tool_calls"]:
            return reply["content"]                         # stop: answer without a tool call
        for call in reply["tool_calls"]:                    # one result per call, same id
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call["id"],
                             "content": execute(tools, call)})
    raise RuntimeError("step budget exhausted")

def execute(tools, call, max_chars=8000):
    try:
        tool = tools[call["name"]]                          # KeyError: hallucinated tool
        args = json.loads(call["arguments"])
        jsonschema.validate(args, tool["parameters"])
        out = tool["fn"](**args)
        text = out if isinstance(out, str) else json.dumps(out, default=str)
    except Exception as e:                                  # errors are observations
        text = f"ERROR {type(e).__name__}: {e}"
    return text[:max_chars]
```

Pitfalls an interviewer checks:

- The assistant message with its tool calls must be appended before the results, and every
  call needs exactly one result with the matching id, or the next request is rejected.
- Tool errors go back to the model as results; only harness faults raise.
- A hard step limit and bounded tool output.

Missing for production: permission and approval checks before side-effecting tools,
per-tool timeouts, retry with backoff on API errors, token and cost budgets, context
compaction, concurrency for parallel-safe calls, an event log for resume, tracing, and a
completion verifier.

**Follow-ups**

- Where would you add human approval, and what is persisted while waiting?
- How would you run the tool calls in parallel safely?

</details>


### Agent frameworks, harnesses and runtimes (LangGraph, LlamaIndex, agent SDKs) <span class="demand">26% of postings</span> {#orchestration}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.orchestration.0"> Name the components of a harness (context compiler, tool executor, state, controller, verifiers, permissions, observability)
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.orchestration.1"> Design sandboxing and a permission policy for an agent that can run shell commands
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.orchestration.2"> Make a long-running agent resumable with an event log, checkpoints and durable human approval
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.orchestration.3"> Say what LangGraph, LlamaIndex, DSPy and vendor agent SDKs each provide
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.orchestration.4"> Argue when to write the loop yourself and what you would then have to rebuild

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-008">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What is an agent harness, and what are its components?</summary>

The harness is everything around the model that turns a next-token predictor into a
closed-loop system: it decides what the model sees, executes what the model proposes, and
enforces what the model must not decide. The same model can score very differently under
different harnesses, which is why postings ask for it by name.

Components:

- **Context compiler**: assembles rules, task, tool definitions, working state, selected
  evidence and recent history for each call; handles ordering, truncation and compaction.
- **Tool registry and executor**: schemas, argument validation, timeouts, output
  normalisation, side-effect class, retry semantics.
- **State and memory**: append-only event log, working state (plan, budgets), artefacts on
  disk, long-term memory.
- **Controller**: the loop itself, with termination conditions, budgets, retries, escalation,
  sub-agent and background-job lifecycles, resume after interruption.
- **Verifiers**: tests, schema checks, citation checks; they turn "I think I am done" into
  evidence.
- **Permission layer**: least privilege, sandboxing, approval for consequential actions;
  outside the model's control.
- **Observability**: traces of every decision, call, result, token count and termination
  reason.

The design rule: deterministic invariants belong in code. Writing "never call more than 20
tools" in a prompt makes a hard rule probabilistic and wastes context.

**Follow-ups**

- Which component would you build first for a new agent, and why?
- What does the harness do that a stronger model will not make unnecessary?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-009">
<summary><span class="tag tag-staff">staff</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Design the harness for a coding agent that works in a developer's repository and can run shell commands.</summary>

**Tools.** Search (grep, glob), read with line ranges, edit by exact string replacement or
patch (cheaper and safer than whole-file rewrites), shell, and a way to run tests. Tool
output is bounded; large output goes to a file the agent can page through.

**Sandbox.** Run commands in a container, VM or OS-level sandbox: file writes limited to
the workspace, network denied by default with an allowlist (package registries), no ambient
credentials in the environment. State which capability sits inside which boundary; an
external MCP tool is not covered by the shell sandbox.

**Permissions.** Rules evaluated in code per action: reads allowed; workspace edits allowed
or ask-once; shell commands matched against allow, ask and deny patterns; pushing, deploying,
deleting outside the workspace and anything touching secrets needs explicit approval. The
effective action set is the intersection of sandbox, rules and approval policy.

**Context.** Load a repository instruction file and a compact environment description;
never load the repo wholesale, search on demand. Keep the prefix stable for caching (fixed
tool order, append-only history). Compact when near the limit, preserving the task, user
constraints, files touched, failing tests and attempted fixes.

**Feedback and verification.** Compilers, type checkers, linters and tests are the dense
signal that makes coding agents work; run them after edits and before claiming done. Show
the diff to the user.

**State.** Append-only event log to replay or resume a session; file snapshots or commits
as checkpoints so any step can be rolled back; explicit interrupt semantics (what happens
to an in-flight command).

**Extras.** Read-only sub-agents for wide searches; hooks before and after tool calls for
policy and formatting; full traces with token and cost accounting.

**Evaluation.** Repository tasks graded by hidden tests in fresh containers, plus tasks
from your own codebase; report resolve rate, cost and time per task, and human
intervention rate.

**Threats.** Injection via repository files, issue text, web pages and dependency docs;
data exfiltration through the network; destructive commands. The sandbox bounds the blast
radius when the prompt-level defences fail.

**Follow-ups**

- Why edit by string replacement instead of rewriting files?
- How would you let the agent work unattended overnight without widening the risk?
- A post-tool hook finds a secret in the diff. What can it still prevent?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-010">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> What do LangGraph, LlamaIndex, DSPy and vendor agent SDKs actually give you, and when would you write the loop yourself?</summary>

What each provides (APIs change quickly, so treat details as version-specific):

- **LangGraph**: a graph or state-machine runtime. Nodes are steps, edges are transitions,
  a typed shared state flows through; checkpointing gives persistence, resume and
  human-in-the-loop interrupts.
- **LlamaIndex**: a data framework for RAG: loaders, parsers and chunkers, indices,
  retrievers, rerankers and query engines, plus agent and workflow abstractions on top.
- **DSPy**: programs written as typed signatures and modules instead of prompt strings;
  optimizers search instructions and few-shot demonstrations against a metric and a
  training set. It needs a metric and data to be useful.
- **Vendor agent SDKs** (OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Google ADK and similar): a
  maintained loop with tool definitions, hand-offs or sub-agents, guardrail hooks, sessions
  and tracing, tuned for that vendor's models.

The core loop is about 50 lines. The hard parts are tool design, context assembly, evals
and permissions, and no framework does those for you.

Write it yourself when you need full control of the exact request sent to the model, when
the abstraction hides prompts or token usage, or when the control flow is unusual. Use a
framework for the commodity runtime you would otherwise rebuild: durable state and resume,
streaming, tracing, connectors.

A practical test: can you print the exact messages and tool definitions for any call, and
can you swap one component without rewriting the rest? If not, the framework will cost more
in debugging than it saves.

**Follow-ups**

- What breaks first when a prototype built on a framework goes to production?
- How would you evaluate a DSPy-optimised prompt against your hand-written one?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-011">
<summary><span class="tag tag-staff">staff</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> An agent run can take hours and includes a step that needs human approval. How do you make it survive crashes, restarts and a two-day wait?</summary>

Model the run as a resumable state machine, not a blocking function call.

**Event log as source of truth.** Append every model response, tool call, tool result,
approval and error to durable storage. State is rebuilt by replaying the log; derived UI
state is a projection, not a second source of truth.

**Checkpoint boundaries.** Persist the model's response before executing its tool calls,
and each tool result as soon as it returns. On restart, completed steps are read from the
log and not re-executed.

**The ambiguous step.** A crash between "tool started" and "result recorded" leaves a side
effect in an unknown state. Handle it with an idempotency key derived from (run id, step,
call id) that the downstream system deduplicates on, or by querying the target's state
before retrying. Without one of these, at-least-once execution means duplicate refunds.

**Durable approval.** A pending approval is a persisted record, not a waiting process:
store the exact proposed action, release compute, resume on an external signal. Bind the
approval to a hash of the arguments so any change needs re-approval; give it an expiry and
a defined behaviour on timeout and on rejection (the model is told and can replan).

**Interruption.** Define what cancel means for the model stream, the in-flight tool,
effects already applied and the next resume. Killing the process is not a design.

**Implementation.** A durable-execution engine (Temporal-style) fits: orchestration code
is deterministic and replayable, while model calls and tools are activities whose recorded
results are replayed rather than recomputed. LangGraph-style checkpointers give a lighter
version of the same idea.

**Follow-ups**

- Why can you not simply re-run the model call during replay?
- The context has been compacted since the checkpoint. What do you restore?

</details>


### Building on model APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock) <span class="demand">25% of postings</span> {#llm-apis}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.llm-apis.0"> Handle rate limits, retries with backoff and jitter, timeouts and streaming errors
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.llm-apis.1"> Check finish reasons (length, tool call, refusal or content filter) before using a response
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.llm-apis.2"> Design provider or model fallback and say why prompts are not portable across models
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.llm-apis.3"> Explain sources of non-determinism and how tests and evals account for it
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.llm-apis.4"> Plan a model version migration with pinned snapshots and a re-qualification eval

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-041">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> What does a production-grade client for a hosted model API need to handle?</summary>

- **Rate limits.** Providers limit requests and tokens per minute, often separately for
  input and output. Handle 429 with the `retry-after` header; add a client-side token
  bucket and a queue with backpressure so bursts wait instead of failing; give interactive
  traffic priority over batch.
- **Retries.** Exponential backoff with jitter for 429, 5xx, timeouts and overload errors,
  with a cap on attempts and total time. Do not retry 4xx validation errors. A retried
  request may be billed twice and returns a different sample.
- **Timeouts and streaming.** Long generations need streaming to avoid idle-connection
  timeouts. Handle errors that arrive mid-stream and decide what to do with partial output.
- **Finish reasons.** Check why generation stopped before using the output: natural end,
  token limit (truncated), tool call, or refusal or content filter.
- **Fallbacks.** A secondary model, region or provider behind a circuit breaker. Prompts
  and tool-call behaviour are not portable across models, so the fallback path needs its
  own prompt tuning and its own eval results.
- **Capacity.** Know your quota against peak tokens per minute; consider provisioned
  throughput for latency-sensitive paths; hedge requests only where tail latency justifies
  the cost.
- **Observability.** Log request id, model version, token counts including cached tokens,
  latency, finish reason and retries for every call.
- **Data terms.** Retention, training use, residency, and what may be sent at all.
- **Versioning.** Pin dated model versions and track deprecation dates.

**Follow-ups**

- You are at the token-per-minute limit at peak. What are your options?
- What can go wrong when failing over to another provider mid-conversation?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-042">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> LLM outputs are non-deterministic and the models behind an API change. How do you build a reliable system on that?</summary>

**Where the variance comes from.** Sampling (temperature, top-p). Even at temperature 0,
outputs can differ between calls: floating-point results depend on batching and hardware,
requests land on different replicas, and providers update serving stacks. Seed parameters
are best effort. Some reasoning models do not expose sampling parameters at all.

**Consequences for testing.**

- Assert properties, not exact strings: schema validity, required facts present, a grader's
  verdict.
- Run each eval case several times and report a pass rate with a confidence interval; a
  case that passes four times in five is a finding in itself.
- Use record-and-replay of model responses for unit tests of the surrounding code.

**Consequences for design.**

- Put anything that must be exact in code: arithmetic, lookups, permission checks.
- Validate outputs and retry within bounds; make downstream actions idempotent.
- Use multiple samples with voting only where the accuracy gain justifies the cost.

**Model changes.**

- Pin dated snapshots; moving aliases change behaviour without a deploy on your side.
- Snapshots are deprecated on a schedule, so migration is recurring work. Keep an eval
  suite that re-qualifies a new model, and expect to re-tune prompts: instructions that
  compensated for the old model can hurt the new one.
- Roll out with shadow traffic or a canary, comparing quality, latency and cost.
- Keep periodic canary prompts in production to detect upstream drift.

The goal is system-level reliability from an unreliable component, the same way
distributed systems treat networks.

**Follow-ups**

- A test passes locally and fails in CI one time in ten. What do you do?
- How do you decide the number of trials per eval case?

</details>


### Prompt and context engineering <span class="demand">22% of postings</span> {#prompting}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.prompting.0"> List what goes into the context window and order it for both quality and cache reuse
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.prompting.1"> Describe compaction strategies and what must survive a summary verbatim
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.prompting.2"> Decide between long-context stuffing, one-shot retrieval and agentic retrieval
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.prompting.3"> Explain prompt caching as a prefix match and name the common silent invalidators
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.prompting.4"> Run prompts as versioned artefacts with a regression suite and pinned model versions
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.prompting.5"> Choose few-shot examples and say when they hurt

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-017">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What goes into the context window of a production LLM feature, and how do you order it?</summary>

Context engineering is choosing the smallest set of high-signal tokens that makes the next
output correct. The layers:

1. **Rules**: role, policies, output contract. Stable and authoritative.
2. **Tool definitions.**
3. **Reference material**: retrieved documents, few-shot examples.
4. **State**: plan, progress, known constraints, open errors.
5. **History**: recent turns and tool results.
6. **The current request.**

Ordering principles:

- *Stable first, volatile last.* Prompt caches match on the prefix, so tools, system prompt
  and fixed documents go first; timestamps, user-specific data and the question go last.
- *Long documents before the question*, with the instruction restated at the end. Models
  attend best to the start and end of long inputs ("lost in the middle"), so do not bury
  the key instruction or the key passage mid-context.
- *Delimit data from instructions* (tags or fenced sections) and label untrusted content
  as data to be analysed, not obeyed.
- *Say why, not just what.* A short reason for a rule generalises better than emphasis.

Few-shot examples: three to five, diverse, covering edge cases, in exactly the output
format you want. For heterogeneous inputs, select examples per request by similarity.
Models copy surface features of examples, so near-identical examples narrow the output.

Failure modes: contradictory instructions accumulated over time, stale retrieved content,
tool outputs that swamp the window, and treating a transcript dump as state.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you test whether an instruction in the prompt is still doing anything?
- When do few-shot examples make outputs worse?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-018">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Your agent's context fills up on long tasks. What are the compaction strategies and what can go wrong?</summary>

Quality degrades before the hard limit: long, noisy contexts make models miss instructions
and reuse stale information. So manage context continuously, not only at overflow.

**Strategies, cheapest first.**

1. *Bound tool output at the source*: return the relevant slice, store the full output as
   an artefact with a pointer.
2. *Clear old tool results*: keep the record that the call happened, drop the bulky payload
   that can be re-fetched.
3. *Summarise history into structured state*: goal, user constraints, decisions and their
   reasons, files or entities touched, open errors, failed attempts, next steps.
4. *Externalise*: write notes or plans to files or a memory store and re-read on demand.
5. *Isolate*: push exploration into a sub-agent that returns only its conclusion.

**What must survive verbatim.** User constraints, the definition of done, unresolved
errors, the reasons earlier approaches failed, and source attributions.

**Costs.** Summaries are lossy, and rewriting history invalidates the prompt cache from
that point, so compaction trades a one-time cache miss for a smaller context. Trigger at a
threshold well below the limit so the summary itself has room.

**Failure modes.** The agent repeats an approach whose failure was summarised away; a
user constraint disappears; the summary states a guess as a fact.

**How to test.** Evals that interrupt a run, compact, and resume; compare task success and
repeated-action rate with and without compaction.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you choose between clearing tool results and summarising?
- What is the compaction analogue of a regression test?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-019">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Context windows now reach a million tokens. Why still build retrieval, and when would you just put everything in the prompt?</summary>

Put it all in the prompt when the corpus is small enough to fit comfortably, changes
rarely, and every user may see all of it. With prompt caching the repeated prefix is cheap
on later requests, there is no retrieval miss, and the model can reason across documents.
This is the right first version for a knowledge base of tens to a few hundred pages.

Build retrieval when any of these holds:

- **Size**: the corpus exceeds the window, or will.
- **Cost and latency**: input cost and time to first token scale with prompt length on
  every request; at high QPS a long prompt per request dominates the bill even with caching.
- **Access control**: different users may see different documents, which breaks a shared
  cached prefix and makes "put everything in" a leak.
- **Freshness**: documents change; re-indexing a changed document is cheaper than
  invalidating a huge cached prompt.
- **Accuracy**: irrelevant material acts as distractors, and recall of a specific fact
  drops as context grows.
- **Attribution**: retrieval gives a natural unit for citations.

Retrieval's weakness is that a one-shot miss is unrecoverable: if the passage is not in
the top k, the model cannot answer. Global questions ("summarise the themes across all
contracts") also do badly with top-k chunks.

The middle option is agentic retrieval: give the model search and read tools and let it
iterate. It recovers from misses and handles multi-hop questions, at the price of more
calls and latency.

Decide from corpus size against window, update rate, QPS times tokens, permission model,
and question types, and confirm with an eval rather than by argument.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you measure the distractor effect on your own data?
- What does per-user access control do to your cache hit rate?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-020">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> How does prompt caching work, and how does it change the way you lay out a prompt?</summary>

The provider stores the model's computed state for a prompt prefix. A later request whose
prompt starts with exactly the same tokens reuses it, so those input tokens are billed at a
discount and time to first token drops.

**It is a prefix match.** A change at any position invalidates everything after it. So the
layout is: tool definitions, then system prompt, then fixed reference material, then
conversation history, then the volatile part (current question, timestamps, per-request
data).

**Silent invalidators.**

- A timestamp, request id or user name near the top of the system prompt.
- Non-deterministic serialisation: unsorted JSON keys, tools listed in varying order.
- Adding or removing a tool mid-conversation.
- Rewriting earlier history (compaction, trimming, editing a message).
- Switching models; caches are per model.

**Provider differences (check current documentation).** Some cache automatically above a
minimum prefix length; others need explicit cache breakpoints. Lifetimes are short,
typically minutes, extended on use. Discounts vary: on Anthropic's API reads cost about a
tenth of the base input price and writes carry a premium of about 25%, so a cached prefix
pays off from the second request.

**Why it matters most for agents.** Each step re-sends the whole history. With an
append-only history, each step pays full price only for the new tokens.

**Operate it.** Log cached versus uncached input tokens per request, track the hit rate,
and alert when it falls; a prompt edit that drops the hit rate to zero can multiply cost
with no visible behaviour change.

**Follow-ups**

- You need the current date in the prompt. Where do you put it?
- How would you inject a new operator instruction mid-conversation without losing the cache?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-021">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> How do you run prompt engineering as an engineering discipline rather than trial and error?</summary>

Treat prompts, tool descriptions and model settings as code with tests.

- **Version control.** Prompts live in the repository as templates, separate from the data
  interpolated into them. Every production trace records the prompt version and the model
  version.
- **Regression suite.** A golden set of inputs with graders (code checks where possible,
  validated LLM judges otherwise) runs on every change. The pull request shows per-slice
  scores and the individual examples that flipped, not only the average.
- **Held-out data.** Tune against a development split and confirm on a held-out split.
  Editing a prompt until five hand-picked examples pass is overfitting.
- **Pinned models.** Use dated model snapshots, not moving aliases. A model upgrade is a
  change like any other: re-run the suite and expect to re-tune, because instructions
  written to compensate for an older model's weaknesses can hurt a newer one.
- **Staged rollout.** Shadow or canary, then A/B on online metrics.
- **Root cause before patching.** When an output is wrong, find out whether it is missing
  context, a conflicting instruction, a retrieval miss or a tool problem. Appending
  "IMPORTANT: never do X" for each incident produces a long, contradictory prompt.
- **Injection surface.** Keep an inventory of every place where user, document or tool
  text is interpolated into the prompt; each is an attack surface and needs delimiting and
  downstream controls.

Automated prompt optimisation (DSPy-style) fits the same frame: it needs a metric and a
dataset, and its output is reviewed and tested like a human-written prompt.

**Follow-ups**

- A prompt change fixes one customer's issue and lowers the suite score by a point. Ship?
- How large does the golden set need to be to detect a 3-point regression?

</details>


### Retrieval-augmented generation <span class="demand">22% of postings</span> {#rag}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.rag.0"> Walk through ingestion, chunking, embedding, hybrid retrieval, reranking, generation and citation
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.rag.1"> Explain how chunk size trades retrieval precision against context and name three chunking strategies
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.rag.2"> Implement reciprocal rank fusion and say why hybrid beats dense-only on identifiers and rare terms
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.rag.3"> Triage a wrong answer into index, retrieval, context assembly or generation failure
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.rag.4"> Enforce document permissions at retrieval time and explain why post-generation filtering is unsafe
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.rag.5"> Evaluate retrieval (recall@k, nDCG) separately from generation (faithfulness, correctness, abstention)

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-022">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Walk me through a RAG system end to end, offline and online, and say where it usually breaks.</summary>

**Offline (ingestion).**

1. *Parse*: PDFs, HTML, slides, tables, scans (OCR). Layout and table extraction quality
   bounds everything downstream.
2. *Chunk*: split into retrievable units, keeping structure (headings, tables, code).
3. *Enrich*: metadata per chunk (source, title, section path, date, version, permissions).
4. *Embed and index*: a vector index plus a lexical (BM25) index.
5. *Keep fresh*: incremental updates from change events, deletions, periodic reconciliation.

**Online (query).**

1. *Query processing*: rewrite a conversational turn into a standalone query; optionally
   decompose or expand.
2. *Retrieve*: top 50-100 candidates from dense and lexical retrieval, with metadata and
   permission filters applied in the retriever.
3. *Rerank*: a cross-encoder or LLM reranker cuts to the best 5-10.
4. *Assemble*: passages with source ids, ordered and deduplicated, within a token budget.
5. *Generate*: answer only from the passages, cite ids, abstain if unsupported.
6. *Check*: citation and groundedness verification before returning.

**Where it breaks.** Most failures are upstream of the model: a table parsed into noise, a
chunk boundary that separates a number from its meaning, a query whose exact identifier
dense retrieval misses, a stale version of a document outranking the current one. Fewer are
generation failures: the model ignores the passage, blends in prior knowledge, or answers
when it should abstain.

Changing the embedding model means re-embedding the whole corpus, so version the index.

**Follow-ups**

- Which stage would you instrument first, and with what metric?
- How do you handle a question the corpus cannot answer?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-023">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> How do you choose a chunking strategy and chunk size?</summary>

Chunk size trades retrieval precision against context. Small chunks give a focused
embedding and precise matches but lose the surrounding meaning ("it increased 12%" with no
subject). Large chunks keep context but dilute the embedding across several topics and
spend prompt tokens on irrelevant text.

A reasonable starting point is a few hundred tokens with 10-20% overlap; treat it as a
hyperparameter and tune on a retrieval eval.

Strategies:

- **Fixed size with overlap**: simple baseline; splits mid-sentence and mid-table.
- **Structure-aware / recursive**: split on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences;
  keep tables, lists and code blocks whole.
- **Semantic**: split where the similarity between adjacent sentences drops.
- **Small-to-big (parent-child)**: index small chunks for matching, return the enclosing
  section to the model.
- **Contextual chunks**: prepend the document title and section path, or a short
  model-written sentence situating the chunk, before embedding. This repairs lost referents.

Choose by document type: structured manuals and code favour structure-aware splitting;
transcripts and prose favour semantic or sliding windows; FAQs are one chunk per question.

Evaluate with recall@k and nDCG on labelled queries, and end-to-end answer correctness.
Looking at a few chunks is not an evaluation.

Failure modes: answers that span a boundary, split tables, overlap that returns the same
text twice, and chunks so short that everything matches weakly.

**Follow-ups**

- Recall@10 is fine but answers lack context. What do you change?
- How does the embedding model's maximum input length constrain your choice?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-024">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Why use hybrid retrieval and a reranker, and when does query rewriting help?</summary>

**Hybrid.** Dense retrieval matches meaning and paraphrase but is weak on exact tokens it
did not learn well: product codes, error strings, rare names, new jargon. Lexical retrieval
(BM25) is the opposite: exact on tokens, blind to synonyms. Their errors are complementary,
so fusing them raises recall. Fuse with reciprocal rank fusion (rank-based, no score
calibration needed) or a weighted sum of normalised scores.

**Reranking.** First-stage retrieval encodes query and document separately (a bi-encoder),
which is fast but coarse. A cross-encoder reads the query and passage together and scores
relevance much more accurately, at one forward pass per candidate. So retrieve 50-200
candidates cheaply and rerank to 5-10. Cost: tens to a few hundred milliseconds, depending
on model size and candidate count.

**Query rewriting.**

- *Standalone rewrite*: resolve "what about the second one?" into a self-contained query.
  Close to mandatory for multi-turn chat.
- *Decomposition*: split a multi-hop question into sub-queries.
- *Expansion*: add synonyms or generate several paraphrases and fuse the results.
- *HyDE*: embed a hypothetical answer instead of the question, which moves the query closer
  to document space.

Rewriting costs an extra model call and can drift from the user's intent, so keep the
original query in the fusion.

Add each stage only if it moves recall@k or nDCG on a labelled set; a reranker on top of
a retriever that misses the document fixes nothing.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you set the candidate depth before reranking?
- When does dense-only retrieval beat hybrid?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-025">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Implement hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion.</summary>

RRF scores a document by its ranks across retrievers:
$\mathrm{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r} \frac{w_r}{k + \mathrm{rank}_r(d)}$, with $k = 60$ by convention
and ranks starting at 1. A document absent from a list contributes nothing for that list.

```python
from collections import defaultdict

def rrf(rankings, k=60, weights=None):
    """rankings: list of ranked lists of doc ids, best first. Returns [(doc_id, score)]."""
    weights = weights or [1.0] * len(rankings)
    scores = defaultdict(float)
    for w, ranking in zip(weights, rankings):
        seen = set()
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            if doc_id in seen:                    # count each doc once per list
                continue
            seen.add(doc_id)
            scores[doc_id] += w / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: (-x[1], str(x[0])))   # deterministic ties

def hybrid_search(query, bm25, embed, ann, top_k=10, depth=100, flt=None):
    lexical = bm25.search(query, depth, filter=flt)           # -> [doc_id, ...]
    dense = ann.search(embed(query), depth, filter=flt)       # -> [doc_id, ...]
    return rrf([lexical, dense])[:top_k]
```

Pitfalls:

- RRF uses ranks only, so it needs no score normalisation but ignores how confident each
  retriever was. A weighted sum of normalised scores can do better if scores are calibrated.
- Fuse at one granularity. If one retriever returns chunks and the other documents, map
  both to the same id first.
- Retrieve deeper than `top_k` from each list, or fusion has nothing to add.
- Apply permission and metadata filters inside each retriever. Filtering after fusion can
  leave fewer than `top_k` results, and for permissions it is the wrong place.
- $k$ damps the influence of top ranks; small $k$ makes rank 1 dominate.
- Tune weights and depth on a labelled set; follow with a reranker if latency allows.

**Follow-ups**

- Why is k around 60 and what happens at k = 0?
- How would you add a third retriever that is much noisier than the other two?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-026">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Implement semantic chunking: split a document where the topic changes, with size limits.</summary>

Embed sentences, measure the cosine distance between neighbours, and cut at the largest
jumps, subject to minimum and maximum chunk sizes.

```python
import re
import numpy as np

def semantic_chunks(text, embed, max_tokens=400, min_tokens=80, pct=90,
                    n_tokens=lambda s: len(s.split())):
    sents = [s.strip() for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text) if s.strip()]
    if len(sents) < 2:
        return sents
    E = np.asarray(embed(sents), dtype=np.float32)                  # (n, d)
    E /= np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-12
    dist = 1.0 - np.sum(E[:-1] * E[1:], axis=1)                     # (n-1,) neighbour distance
    thresh = np.percentile(dist, pct)                               # cut at the largest jumps
    chunks, cur, cur_len = [], [sents[0]], n_tokens(sents[0])
    for i in range(1, len(sents)):
        n = n_tokens(sents[i])
        topic_shift = dist[i - 1] > thresh and cur_len >= min_tokens
        if topic_shift or cur_len + n > max_tokens:
            chunks.append(" ".join(cur))
            cur, cur_len = [], 0
        cur.append(sents[i])
        cur_len += n
    chunks.append(" ".join(cur))
    return chunks
```

Pitfalls:

- Single-sentence embeddings are noisy. Embedding a sliding window of two or three
  sentences around each position gives steadier boundaries.
- The percentile threshold is relative to the document, so a single-topic document is
  still cut at its top 10% of jumps; the minimum size limits the damage.
- A single sentence longer than `max_tokens` still needs a hard split.
- The regex splitter breaks on abbreviations, decimals, code and tables. Split on structure
  (headings, tables, code blocks) first and apply this within sections.
- Count tokens with the embedding model's tokenizer, not whitespace.
- Ingestion cost is one embedding per sentence.
- Semantic chunking does not always beat structure-aware fixed-size chunking. Compare
  recall@k on labelled queries before adopting it.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you add overlap or parent-child retrieval to this?
- What is the time complexity, and where is the cost in practice?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-027">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Users report that your RAG assistant gives confidently wrong answers. How do you find the cause and fix it?</summary>

Take a sample of wrong answers with their traces and assign each to the first stage that
failed:

1. **Not in the index**: the document was never ingested, was parsed badly (tables, scans),
   or is stale.
2. **Indexed but not retrieved**: not in the top k. Vocabulary mismatch, an exact identifier
   dense retrieval missed, a bad chunk boundary, an over-restrictive filter.
3. **Retrieved but not in the prompt**: dropped by the reranker or the token budget.
4. **In the prompt but answered wrongly**: the model ignored it, blended in prior knowledge,
   or picked one of two conflicting or outdated passages.
5. **Unanswerable**: the corpus has no answer and the model produced one anyway.

The distribution across buckets tells you where to work. Prompt edits only help buckets 4
and 5.

Fixes by bucket: better parsing and freshness monitoring (1); hybrid retrieval, query
rewriting, chunking changes (2); deeper candidates, reranker tuning, larger budget (3);
instructions to answer only from sources, recency and authority metadata, deduplication
of versions (4); explicit abstention plus an answerability check (5).

For the "confidently" part:

- Require a citation per claim and verify after generation that each cited passage
  supports its claim (entailment model or LLM judge); block or flag unsupported claims.
- Abstain when retrieval scores are low or passages disagree.
- Show sources to the user.

Then keep it fixed: put the failures into the regression set, and track retrieval recall
and groundedness on sampled production traffic.

**Follow-ups**

- Two retrieved documents contradict each other. What should the system do?
- How do you measure abstention quality without making the system refuse everything?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-028">
<summary><span class="tag tag-staff">staff</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Design enterprise RAG over documents with access controls (SharePoint, Drive, Confluence, Slack) for a company with tens of thousands of employees.</summary>

**Requirements to pin down.** Sources and volume, freshness target for content and for
permission changes, the non-negotiable (a user never sees content they cannot open at
source), citations, audit, tenancy and data residency.

**Ingestion.** One connector per source with incremental sync (change feeds or webhooks)
and a periodic full reconcile to catch missed events and deletions. Each document is
stored with its ACL: users, groups, inheritance and link-sharing rules. Source principals
are mapped to one company identity; group membership is synced separately because it
changes without the document changing.

**Enforcing permissions.** Filter at retrieval, before anything reaches the model. Content
the user may not see must never enter the context window; a model cannot be trusted to
withhold what it has read.

- *Index-time ACLs*: store allowed principals on each chunk and filter by the user's
  expanded principal set. Fast, but stale until the next sync.
- *Query-time check*: confirm the top results against the source system. Always current,
  but slower.
- Use both: filter in the index, then verify the final few results at source.

Revocation latency is a stated SLO. Response caches and semantic caches are keyed by
permission scope or disabled.

**Retrieval and generation.** Structure-aware chunking with title and path context; hybrid
retrieval with filter-aware ANN, falling back to exact search when a user's permitted set
is small; reranking; generation with citations that link to the source, which re-checks
access.

**Security.** Documents are untrusted input (indirect injection), so the answering model
gets no write tools. Per-tenant isolation. Audit log of who queried and which documents
were retrieved. PII handling and retention.

**Evaluation.** Per-source retrieval sets; a permission test suite with canary documents
that specific test users must never retrieve, run continuously; groundedness and citation
accuracy; freshness lag dashboards.

**Scale risks.** Group fan-out for users in thousands of groups, very selective filters
degrading ANN recall, and re-embedding the corpus on a model change.

**Follow-ups**

- A user is removed from a group. Walk me through what must happen and how fast.
- Why is filtering the generated answer not sufficient?
- How would you test for a permission leak before launch?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-029">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> How do you evaluate a RAG system? Be specific about retrieval versus generation.</summary>

Evaluate the stages separately, then end to end, because an end-to-end score cannot tell
you which stage to fix.

**Retrieval.** Labelled pairs of query and relevant chunk or document ids.

- recall@k: is the needed passage among the k passed on? This caps answer quality.
- MRR or nDCG@k: is it ranked high enough to survive truncation?
- Report by query type (lookup, multi-hop, identifier, conversational).

**Generation, given the retrieved context.**

- *Faithfulness / groundedness*: is every claim supported by the provided passages?
- *Answer correctness* against a reference answer.
- *Citation precision and recall*: do citations support the claims, and are claims cited?
- *Abstention*: on unanswerable questions, does it decline; on answerable ones, does it not?

**Diagnostic matrix.** Cross retrieval hit or miss with answer right or wrong. A hit with
a wrong answer is a generation problem; a miss with a right answer means the model used
prior knowledge, which is a risk; a miss with a wrong answer is a retrieval problem.

**Building the set.** Sample real queries and have experts label; include unanswerable,
multi-hop and ambiguous queries. Synthetic questions generated from chunks are useful for
volume but are lexically close to their source and overstate retrieval quality.

**Graders.** Retrieval metrics are computed in code. Faithfulness and correctness usually
need an LLM judge, validated against human labels before it is trusted.

**Online.** Citation click-through, reformulation rate, thumbs, escalation to a human, and
sampled traces scored by the same graders.

**Follow-ups**

- Your labelled set only marks one relevant chunk per query but several exist. What happens to your metrics?
- How would you get retrieval labels cheaply?

</details>


### Tool use, function calling, MCP <span class="demand">21% of postings</span> {#tool-use}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.tool-use.0"> Explain the function-calling protocol end to end, including how tool results are paired with calls
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.tool-use.1"> Design a tool schema that is hard to misuse (enums, required fields, non-overlapping tools, compact results)
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.tool-use.2"> Classify tools by side effect and make retried writes idempotent
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.tool-use.3"> Decide which parallel tool calls may run concurrently and how partial failures are reported
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.tool-use.4"> Describe what MCP standardises (tools, resources, prompts, transports, authorization) and its security concerns
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.tool-use.5"> Say when computer or browser use is justified over an API tool and how to contain it

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-012">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> How does function calling work, and what makes a tool definition good?</summary>

**Mechanism.** You send tool definitions (name, description, JSON Schema for parameters)
with the request; they are rendered into the model's context. The model either answers in
text or emits a structured call (tool name plus JSON arguments). The model executes
nothing: your code parses the call, runs the function and sends the result back as a tool
message tied to the call id, and the model continues. Tool definitions cost input tokens
on every request.

**What makes a definition good.**

- *Few, non-overlapping tools.* Two tools that could both apply create selection errors.
  Prefer one task-shaped tool (`get_order_status`) over thin wrappers around three endpoints.
- *Descriptions written for a newcomer*: what it does, when to use it, when not to, what it
  returns, with an example for tricky arguments.
- *Tight schemas*: enums instead of free strings, required fields, explicit formats (ISO
  dates, ids), flat rather than deeply nested. Make invalid states hard to express.
- *Results designed for the model*: compact, stable field names, ids that can be passed to
  the next call, pagination or truncation with a note that more exists.
- *Declared side-effect class*: read, reversible write, irreversible action.

Schema-constrained ("strict") tool calling, where the provider supports it, guarantees
arguments parse and match the schema. It does not guarantee they are correct, so validate
semantics and authorisation server-side.

With dozens of tools, selection accuracy drops and definitions crowd the context: namespace
them, load definitions on demand through a tool-search step, or route to a subset.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you find out that two tool descriptions are confusing the model?
- Why return ids rather than names in tool results?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-013">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Talk me through error handling, parallel tool calls and idempotency in a tool executor.</summary>

**Validation before execution.** Check arguments against the schema, then semantics
(ranges, existence) and authorisation (does this user own this resource). The model's
arguments are untrusted input.

**Three error classes.**

- *Transient* (timeout, 429, 5xx): the harness retries with backoff; the model need not know
  unless retries are exhausted.
- *Model-fixable* (bad argument, not found, precondition failed): return as a tool result
  saying what failed and what a valid call looks like, so the model can correct itself.
- *Fatal* (auth revoked, invariant violated, policy denial): stop or escalate; do not let
  the model work around it.

**Parallel calls.** Models often emit several calls in one turn. Run them concurrently only
when their effects commute: reads in parallel, writes serialised. Whether a tool is
parallel-safe is metadata on the tool, decided in code. Return a result for every call,
including failures, each tied to its call id.

**Idempotency.** A timed-out write may have succeeded. Retrying a payment, an email or a
deploy can duplicate it. Options: an idempotency key per logical action that the downstream
system deduplicates on; check-then-act (read current state before retrying); or a
two-phase prepare-and-confirm for irreversible actions. Retried model turns can also
re-propose the same action, so dedupe at the action level, not only the HTTP level.

**Bounds.** Per-tool timeouts, output size caps, and rate limits per run.

**Follow-ups**

- The downstream API has no idempotency support. What do you do?
- One of four parallel calls fails. What does the model see?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-014">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> What is the Model Context Protocol, what does it standardise, and what are its security concerns?</summary>

MCP is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 and since adopted by other
vendors, for connecting LLM applications to external tools and data. It turns the M x N
integration problem (every app times every system) into M + N: a system exposes one MCP
server, and any MCP-capable host can use it.

**Architecture.** A host application (IDE, chat app, agent runtime) runs MCP clients, each
holding a connection to one server. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0, with capability negotiation
at initialisation.

**Server primitives.**

- *Tools*: functions the model can call, with a name, description and JSON Schema input.
- *Resources*: data the application can read into context (files, records), addressed by URI.
- *Prompts*: reusable templates the user can invoke.

Clients can offer features back to servers, such as sampling (the server asks the host's
model for a completion) and roots (which directories are in scope).

**Transports.** stdio for local servers started as subprocesses, and Streamable HTTP for
remote servers (it replaced the earlier HTTP+SSE transport). Remote authorization is based
on OAuth 2.1. The specification is still evolving, so check the current revision.

**Security concerns.**

- Tool descriptions and tool results are untrusted text that enters the model's context:
  a malicious or compromised server can inject instructions ("tool poisoning").
- A server holds real credentials; over-broad scopes and token pass-through create
  confused-deputy problems.
- A local stdio server runs with the user's privileges.
- The host's sandbox does not automatically cover what an MCP server does.

Mitigations: allowlist servers, pin versions, least-privilege scopes, per-tool approval
for writes, and treat everything returned as data.

**Follow-ups**

- How is an MCP tool different from a function you define in the request?
- Fifty MCP servers are connected and tool definitions fill the context. What do you do?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-015">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Two percent of your agent's tool calls are malformed. How do you investigate and fix it?</summary>

Two percent per call is not small: over a 20-call trajectory the chance of at least one
malformed call is $1 - 0.98^{20} \approx 33\%$.

**Classify the failures from logs first.**

- *Invalid JSON*: usually truncation (finish reason is `length`), or unescaped quotes and
  newlines inside long string arguments such as code or documents.
- *Schema-invalid*: missing required field, wrong type, invented enum value.
- *Unknown tool name*: hallucinated or from a stale tool list.
- *Client bug*: streamed argument deltas concatenated in the wrong order or across calls.

**Look for what the failures correlate with.** One tool, long arguments, long context,
parallel calls, a model version, streaming versus non-streaming.

**Fixes, most effective first.**

1. Turn on schema-constrained (strict) tool calling if the provider offers it; this removes
   syntax and schema errors, except truncation.
2. Raise the output token limit, and treat `length` as an error rather than parsing a
   partial call.
3. Simplify the schema: flatten nesting, fewer optional fields, enums, and move large
   payloads out of JSON (write to a file, pass a reference).
4. Validate before execution and return the validation error to the model for one bounded
   repair attempt.
5. Fix the streaming accumulator (key deltas by call index).
6. Tighten the description, add one example of a correct call.

Then make the malformed-call rate a tracked metric per tool and per model version, alert on
it, and add the failing inputs to the regression suite so a model or prompt change that
brings it back is caught.

**Follow-ups**

- Constrained decoding is on and you still see failures. What are they?
- Why not just retry the whole request?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-016">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> When would you give an agent computer or browser use instead of API tools, and how do you contain it?</summary>

Computer use means the model perceives a screen (screenshots, sometimes with a DOM or
accessibility tree) and emits mouse and keyboard actions in a perceive-act loop. It is the
tool of last resort: use it when the target has no API (legacy desktop software, third-party
sites, UI testing).

**Order of preference.** A structured API tool; then browser automation over the DOM or
accessibility tree (text is cheaper and more reliable to ground than pixels); then
pixel-level control.

**Why it is last.**

- *Slow*: every step is a screenshot plus a model call, so seconds per action and minutes
  per task.
- *Expensive*: image tokens on every step.
- *Brittle*: layout changes, pop-ups, loading states, mis-grounded click coordinates.
- *Hard to verify*: success must be checked from the resulting state, not from the model's
  claim.
- *Large attack surface*: any text on any page is a potential injected instruction, and the
  agent may hold a logged-in session.

**Containment.** Run in an isolated VM or a dedicated browser profile with no ambient
credentials; allowlist domains; require human confirmation for logins, purchases, sending
messages and anything irreversible; cap steps and time; record the session; verify the end
state with an independent check.

**Evaluation.** Task success on sandboxed, resettable sites or VMs, with steps and cost per
task; expect high run-to-run variance, so run each task several times.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you check that a form was actually submitted?
- What would you do about a page that tells the agent to email its cookies somewhere?

</details>


### Workflow automation and enterprise integration <span class="demand">17% of postings</span> {#workflow-automation}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.workflow-automation.0"> Split a business process into deterministic steps and model steps
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.workflow-automation.1"> Choose between delegated user credentials and a service account and keep credentials away from the model
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.workflow-automation.2"> Make writes to systems of record idempotent and auditable
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.workflow-automation.3"> Place human review using confidence and impact thresholds and feed corrections back into evals

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-043">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> A finance team wants to automate invoice processing into their ERP with an LLM. How do you design the integration?</summary>

**Map the process first.** Receive, extract fields, match to purchase order, validate,
approve, post to the ERP, handle exceptions. Use the model where judgment or unstructured
input is involved (reading the document, classifying exceptions, drafting a query to the
vendor). Keep matching rules, tolerances, approval limits and posting in code.

**Architecture.** An event (new email or upload) starts a durable workflow. Each model step
returns schema-constrained output with supporting quotes; code validates it (totals add
up, vendor exists, PO matches within tolerance). Passing items post through the ERP API;
failing or low-confidence items go to a review queue with the evidence shown.

**Auth and permissions.** The workflow, not the model, holds credentials. Use delegated
user tokens (OAuth, least scopes) when acting for a person, or a service account with
narrowly scoped rights for back-office automation. The ERP still enforces its own
authorisation; the model never sees secrets.

**Idempotency.** Every write carries a key derived from the business object (invoice id
plus action), with a dedupe check, so retries and replays cannot double-post. Multi-step
updates need compensation steps.

**Audit.** Record for each item: inputs, extracted values and quotes, model and prompt
versions, validation results, who approved, and what was written. Auditors must be able to
reconstruct why an invoice was paid.

**Human review.** Thresholds on confidence and amount; reviewer corrections are captured
as labelled data for evals and prompt improvement.

**Integration realities.** API rate limits, pagination, schema changes, duplicate
documents, and documents in formats the parser has not seen.

**Rollout and metrics.** Shadow mode against human decisions, then auto-post the
high-confidence segment. Track straight-through rate, error rate from sampled audits,
cycle time and cost per invoice.

**Follow-ups**

- How do you set the confidence threshold for auto-posting?
- The ERP API times out after you send a post request. What happens next?

</details>


### Guardrails, safety filters, hallucination control <span class="demand">16% of postings</span> {#guardrails}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.guardrails.0"> Define direct and indirect prompt injection and explain why prompting alone cannot prevent it
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.guardrails.1"> State the combination of capabilities that makes exfiltration possible and how to break it
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.guardrails.2"> Lay out input, tool-boundary, output and system-level controls and the latency each adds
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.guardrails.3"> Describe hallucination controls (grounding, citations, abstention, verification)
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="llmapp.guardrails.4"> Measure a guardrail with both attack success rate and false positive rate on benign traffic

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-033">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> What is prompt injection, what is indirect prompt injection, and why can you not fix it with a better system prompt?</summary>

A language model receives instructions and data in one token stream and has no reliable
way to tell them apart. Prompt injection exploits this.

- **Direct injection**: the user writes text that overrides the application's instructions
  ("ignore the above and..."). A *jailbreak* is the related attack on the model's own
  safety policy rather than the application's instructions.
- **Indirect injection**: the instructions are planted in content the system reads on the
  user's behalf: a web page, email, document, code comment, tool result or tool description.
  The user is the victim, not the attacker.

A stronger system prompt or delimiters around untrusted text lowers the success rate but
does not make it zero, and an attacker can retry. So assume some injections succeed and
limit what a successful one can do.

The dangerous combination is an agent that has all three of: access to private data,
exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out (web requests, email, rendering
a URL or image). Remove one and exfiltration is blocked.

Defence in depth:

- Least-privilege tools; read-only where possible.
- Human approval for consequential or outbound actions.
- Egress control: allowlisted domains, no auto-rendering of model-produced links or images.
- Isolation: a quarantined model reads untrusted content and returns constrained data to a
  privileged one that never sees the raw text.
- Taint tracking: once untrusted content is in context, restrict the tools available.
- Injection classifiers on inputs and tool results, as one layer.
- Logging and a red-team suite that measures attack success rate.

**Follow-ups**

- Your agent summarises a web page and can send email. What is the attack and what do you remove?
- Why does markdown image rendering matter?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="llmapp-034">
<summary><span class="tag tag-staff">staff</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> Design the guardrails for an LLM assistant that answers from company data and can take actions. What are the layers and how do you know they work?</summary>

No single filter is sufficient; each layer covers failures the others miss.

| Layer | Controls | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| Input | abuse and rate limits, moderation classifier, PII detection, injection classifier | abusive or policy-violating requests, bulk probing |
| Model | system policy, a model version with tested refusal behaviour | most ordinary misuse |
| Data and tool boundary | permission-filtered retrieval, tool allowlists, argument validation, sandbox, approval for writes | injection consequences, data leaks, wrong actions |
| Output | schema validation, groundedness check against sources, PII and secret scan, moderation | hallucinated claims, leaked data, harmful text |
| System | audit log, monitoring, kill switch, incident process | what slipped through |

**Hallucination control** sits mainly at the output and data layers: answer only from
retrieved sources with citations, abstain when support is missing, verify claims against
their cited passages, choose from enumerated values instead of free text, and compute
numbers in code.

**PII.** Redact in logs and traces by default, minimise what is sent to the model, and
respect retention and residency terms.

**Latency and UX trade-offs.** Run input checks in parallel with generation and cancel on
a hit. Output checks conflict with streaming: check per sentence or buffer, or accept a
